name: Anonymous Mandiant two-persona post-hire incident

attribution.legal_posture: First-party Mandiant responder account and source-attributed DPRK IT-worker assessment; the source scope is responder reporting and IT-worker assessment, with charge, adjudication, sanctions designation, civil-identity finding, and named-victim report outside the source.

caveats: AnyDesk, Astrill VPN, Caffeine, shared egress, address mismatch, rapid tool installation, and camera behavior are contextual signals that require corroboration for DPRK affiliation or fraud.
Controls must be fair, job-relevant, consistently applied, and grounded in job evidence rather than nationality, ethnicity, accent, language, appearance, or other protected traits.
The source records an incident-specific negative finding for theft, exfiltration, sabotage, malware, and other malicious conduct.
Mandiant left unresolved whether the employer-facing communicator was the worker or a facilitator.
Mandiant left unresolved whether the person who communicated with the employer was the underlying worker or a facilitator.
Explicit negative finding: Mandiant's incident account reports zero theft, exfiltration, sabotage, malware, or other malicious conduct.
Explicit negative finding: the record retains no employee, stolen-identity victim, employer, address, IP address, LinkedIn profile, image, or other identifying selector.
The account leaves unresolved whether the two employment personas represented two distinct human operators.
The Apple Podcasts, Buzzsprout audio, RSS, and YouTube endpoints belong to one episode/document family; source-family count is one.
The employer, employment personas, and stolen-identity victim are anonymous; identity resolution and victim deanonymization remain outside the record.
The source-specific observation that one persona appeared on camera and a second rarely did is a local observation; deepfake or attribution rules require broader validation.
This is one Mandiant responder's account and a source-attributed DPRK assessment; adjudication, sanctions designation, and public civil-identity findings require separate sources.
Two employment personas reflect the speaker's assessment that one person operated multiple personas.

statements: At 02:16–03:58, Mandiant responder JP Glab says an employer learned that an employee used a false identity after the identity-theft victim received an unexpected W-2; the first employment persona had performed front- and back-end development for about six months and had referred a second persona who was also hired.

At 04:35–06:29, Mandiant correlated both managed devices using the same external point of presence despite their claimed locations, observed AnyDesk and Astrill VPN, and learned through a parallel HR and legal review that shipping-address information did not align and both devices ultimately appeared in Nevada.

At 07:20–08:36, returned-device review found access to multiple LinkedIn personas, including profiles unknown to the employer, and artifacts showing AnyDesk and Caffeine installed within hours of onboarding; Glab assessed that one operator was using multiple personas.

At 09:43–10:51, Glab says the employment personas were terminated and emphasizes that Mandiant did not necessarily find malicious activity in this incident: the workers performed their jobs and appeared primarily motivated by salary.

At 11:23–15:20, Glab discusses post-hire monitoring of unauthorized applications, consumer VPN use and impossible-travel patterns, pre-hire verification, first-day presence as a possible control, source-specific camera behavior, and the W-2 anomaly as the event that exposed the incident.

sources.support: Mandiant incident responder JP Glab recounts an anonymous employer investigation involving two employment personas. He says a stolen-identity victim's unexpected W-2 triggered the inquiry after the first persona had worked for about six months and referred the second. Mandiant correlated shared egress, AnyDesk and Astrill VPN use, device-shipping discrepancies, multiple LinkedIn personas, and rapid post-onboarding installation of AnyDesk and Caffeine. Glab says the personas were terminated and, crucially, that the workers in this incident were not necessarily conducting malicious activity: they performed their development work and appeared primarily motivated by salary. Evidence boundary: First-party responder account of an anonymous customer engagement and Mandiant's DPRK IT-worker assessment. It is not an adjudication, sanctions designation, public identity finding, or proof that any one observed signal independently establishes attribution
